chapter_title: Special Phrases, Idioms and Completing Sentences

questions.question: Fill in the blank with the appropriate special phrase: 'I ______ starve than steal from another person.'
questions.explanation: 'Would rather... than...' is the standard idiomatic construction expressing strong personal preference between two choices.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'The sky is overcast with dark storm clouds; you ______ take an umbrella with you.'
questions.explanation: 'Had better' gives strong practical advice or warning about an immediate situation, followed by a bare infinitive ('take').

questions.question: What verb form directly follows 'had better' in standard English?

options.label: A
options.text: Bare infinitive (base form of verb without 'to')

questions.correct_answer_text: Bare infinitive (base form of verb without 'to')
questions.explanation: 'Had better' functions as a modal auxiliary and takes the bare infinitive ('You had better leave now').

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'would rather' to express preference?

options.label: A
options.text: She would rather stay at home than go to the cinema tonight.

options.label: B
options.text: She would rather to stay at home than going.

options.label: C
options.text: She would rather staying at home than go.

options.label: D
options.text: She had rather stay at home to go.

questions.correct_answer_text: She would rather stay at home than go to the cinema tonight.
questions.explanation: Both verbs linked by 'would rather... than...' must be in the bare infinitive ('stay... go').

questions.question: When 'would rather' is followed by a subordinate subject clause (expressing a wish about someone else's action), what tense is used?

options.label: A
options.text: Past subjunctive (e.g. 'I would rather you didn't smoke here')

questions.correct_answer_text: Past subjunctive (e.g. 'I would rather you didn't smoke here')
questions.explanation: When 'would rather' has a different grammatical subject in the subordinate clause, it takes the past tense to express present/future preference.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'He cannot afford to buy a second-hand bicycle, ______ a brand-new luxury car.'
questions.explanation: 'Let alone' is used after a negative statement to emphasize that something even more extreme or difficult is utterly out of the question.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '______ the connecting flight gets delayed due to the snowstorm?'
questions.explanation: 'What if' introduces a hypothetical question expressing worry, concern, or speculation about a potential future event.

questions.question: 'The elderly patient cannot walk ten paces unassisted, ______ run a marathon.'
questions.explanation: 'Let alone' highlights the impossibility of running a marathon given that the person cannot even walk ten steps.

questions.question: What communicative function does 'what if' perform in conversation?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypothetical inquiry or suggesting possibilities with apprehension

options.label: D
options.text: Ordering a meal in a restaurant

questions.correct_answer_text: Hypothetical inquiry or suggesting possibilities with apprehension
questions.explanation: 'What if' poses a speculative scenario ('What will happen if...?') often reflecting anxiety or creative consideration.

questions.question: Choose the correctly formed sentence with 'let alone':

options.label: A
options.text: The little child cannot even recite the alphabet, let alone read an entire English novel.

options.label: B
options.text: The little child can read an entire novel, let alone recite the alphabet.

options.label: C
options.text: Let alone the child cannot recite the alphabet.

options.label: D
options.text: The child cannot recite the alphabet what if an English novel.

questions.correct_answer_text: The little child cannot even recite the alphabet, let alone read an entire English novel.
questions.explanation: 'Let alone' progresses from the simpler negative premise to the far more improbable accomplishment.

topics.topic_name: Special Uses - 'Was Born' and 'Have to / Has to'

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'Kazi Nazrul Islam, the national poet of Bangladesh, ______ in Churulia in 1899.'
questions.explanation: 'Was born' is the standard passive idiom used to denote the historical birth of a person in a specific time or place.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'The semester examination begins tomorrow morning; the students ______ study tonight.'
questions.explanation: 'Have to' expresses external necessity or compulsory obligation imposed by circumstances.

questions.question: Choose the correct phrase: 'A candidate ______ secure at least 40% marks to qualify for the next interview.'
questions.explanation: A singular 3rd-person subject ('A candidate') requires 'has to' to denote an institutional requirement.

questions.question: In biographical narratives, which tense does the passive verb 'was born' strictly reflect?
questions.explanation: 'Was born' is structurally a past simple passive form of the archaic verb 'bear' (to bring forth a child).

questions.question: How does 'have to' differ subtly from 'must' in formal English grammar?

options.label: A
options.text: 'Must' reflects internal subjective obligation from the speaker, while 'have to' reflects external objective necessity

options.label: C
options.text: 'Have to' is only used in past tense

options.label: D
options.text: There is no difference in formal grammar

questions.correct_answer_text: 'Must' reflects internal subjective obligation from the speaker, while 'have to' reflects external objective necessity
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses personal determination ('I must do this'), while 'have to' expresses external rules/regulations ('We have to wear uniforms').

topics.topic_name: Special Uses - 'What Does... Look Like' and 'What's It Like'

questions.question: Fill in the blanks: '______ a prehistoric dinosaur ______?' asked the curious child.
questions.explanation: 'What does... look like?' inquires about the visual physical appearance of an object, animal, or person.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: '______ swimming in the cool waters of a mountain stream on a hot summer day?'
questions.explanation: 'What's it like + gerund (-ing)?' inquires about a sensory or emotional experience ('How does it feel to do something?').

questions.question: '______ your new English professor ______? Is he tall and bearded?'
questions.explanation: Because the follow-up asks about physical traits ('tall and bearded'), 'What does... look like?' is the appropriate construction.

questions.question: What is the crucial difference between 'What does he look like?' and 'What is he like?'

options.label: A
options.text: 'What does he look like?' asks about physical appearance; 'What is he like?' asks about personality and character

options.label: B
options.text: 'What is he like?' asks about his salary

options.label: C
options.text: They both ask about height only

options.label: D
options.text: 'What does he look like?' is an informal slang expression

questions.correct_answer_text: 'What does he look like?' asks about physical appearance; 'What is he like?' asks about personality and character
questions.explanation: Appearance is queried by 'look like', while character/temperament is queried by 'be like'.

questions.question: Complete the dialogue: '______ traveling alone in a foreign country without knowing the local language?'
questions.explanation: 'What's it like + traveling...' asks for a description of what that unique experience feels like.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with introductory 'there': '______ are sixty-four districts in Bangladesh.'
questions.explanation: Introductory (existential) 'There' introduces the existence of things, followed here by the plural verb 'are'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank with impersonal 'it': '______ is raining cats and dogs outside.'
questions.explanation: Impersonal or dummy 'It' is used as a formal subject for statements regarding weather, time, distance, and temperature.

questions.question: '______ was once a wise hermit who lived in a secluded cave.'
questions.explanation: 'There was once...' is the standard narrative opening introducing the presence of a person or setting.

questions.question: '______ is twenty kilometers from the city center to the new international airport.'
questions.explanation: Impersonal 'It' is required when stating distances ('It is 20 km from X to Y').

questions.question: In the sentence 'It was Bangabandhu who inspired the nation in 1971', what grammatical structure is 'It was... who...'?

options.label: A
options.text: A Cleft Sentence used for focal emphasis

questions.correct_answer_text: A Cleft Sentence used for focal emphasis
questions.explanation: An 'it-cleft' sentence splits a single clause to place strong dramatic focus on a particular element (Bangabandhu).

topics.topic_name: Completing Sentences with 'So That' and 'In Order That'

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'He studies diligently so that he ______ secure first division in the board examination.'
questions.explanation: When the main clause is in the present tense ('He studies'), 'so that' is followed by 'can' or 'may' + base verb.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'The farmer worked hard in order that he ______ feed his large family.' (Main clause in past tense)
questions.explanation: When the main clause is in the past tense ('worked'), the purpose clause after 'in order that' takes 'could' or 'might'.

questions.question: 'We eat a balanced diet so that we ______ maintain good physical health.'
questions.explanation: 'So that' expressing intended purpose after a present verb ('eat') takes 'may' or 'can'.

questions.question: What is the structural difference between 'so... that' and 'so that'?

options.label: A
options.text: 'So... that' expresses degree and result, while 'so that' expresses purpose

options.label: B
options.text: 'So that' requires an adjective in the middle

options.label: C
options.text: 'So... that' is only used in poetry

questions.correct_answer_text: 'So... that' expresses degree and result, while 'so that' expresses purpose
questions.explanation: 'He was so weak that he could not walk' (result of degree) vs 'He rested so that he could recover' (purpose).

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'The runner sprinted with all his might so that he ______ break the national record.'
questions.explanation: Past tense verb 'sprinted' in the principal clause matches with 'might' in the subordinate purpose clause.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'Walk cautiously on the icy pavement lest you ______ slip and fall.'
questions.explanation: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' or 'to avoid the risk of', and its clause is traditionally formed with 'should + base verb'.

questions.question: Why is the use of 'not' grammatically FORBIDDEN in a clause governed by 'unless'?

options.label: A
options.text: Because 'unless' already has a negative meaning ('if not'), creating an erroneous double negative

options.label: D
options.text: Because 'unless' must always end a sentence

questions.correct_answer_text: Because 'unless' already has a negative meaning ('if not'), creating an erroneous double negative
questions.explanation: 'Unless' inherently means 'if not'; adding 'not' in the same clause (e.g. 'unless you do not study') produces an incorrect double negative.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'Wait in the library until I ______ back from the laboratory.'
questions.explanation: Clauses of time and condition after 'until', 'when', or 'as soon as' take the present simple tense when referring to future actions.

questions.question: 'You will fail in the final evaluation unless you ______ regularly.'
questions.explanation: 'Unless you study' correctly means 'If you do not study'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence with 'lest':

options.label: A
options.text: He hid behind the curtain lest the guards should spot him.

options.label: B
options.text: He hid behind the curtain lest the guards should not spot him.

options.label: C
options.text: He hid behind the curtain lest the guards will spot him.

options.label: D
options.text: He hid behind the curtain lest the guards did not spot him.

questions.correct_answer_text: He hid behind the curtain lest the guards should spot him.
questions.explanation: 'Lest' must not contain another negative word like 'not', making option A the only grammatically correct sentence.

topics.topic_name: Correlative Adverbs - 'No Sooner Had', 'Scarcely Had', 'Hardly Had'

questions.question: Complete the correlative pair: 'No sooner had the bell rung ______ the students rushed out of the classroom.'
questions.explanation: The comparative adverb 'sooner' is strictly correlated with 'than' ('No sooner had... than...').

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'Hardly had we reached the terminal ______ the express bus departed.'
questions.explanation: 'Hardly had...' and 'Scarcely had...' are always correlated with 'when' (or 'before'), never 'than'.

questions.question: What is the tense of the second clause in: 'No sooner had the thief seen the police than he (run) ______ away'?
questions.explanation: The clause following 'than' or 'when' takes the simple past tense ('ran').

questions.question: Why does subject-auxiliary inversion ('had the bell rung') occur after 'No sooner' at the start of a sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: Because negative and restrictive adverbs placed sentence-initially trigger grammatical inversion

options.label: B
options.text: Because it is an interrogative question

options.label: D
options.text: Inversion is purely optional in slang

questions.correct_answer_text: Because negative and restrictive adverbs placed sentence-initially trigger grammatical inversion
questions.explanation: Fronted negative adverbs (No sooner, Hardly, Scarcely, Never) trigger subject-auxiliary inversion in formal English.

questions.question: 'As soon as the teacher entered the classroom, the students ______ silent.'
questions.explanation: In sentences with 'As soon as', both clauses typically share the simple past tense without inversion ('entered... became').

topics.topic_name: Conditional Sentence Completions (Provided That, In Case)

questions.question: Fill in the blank: 'You will easily pass the driving test provided that you ______ all traffic guidelines.'
questions.explanation: 'Provided that' functions as a conditional conjunction meaning 'on condition that / if', taking the present simple tense ('follow').

questions.question: 'Take an umbrella with you in case it ______ later this afternoon.'
questions.explanation: 'In case' expresses precaution against a potential occurrence and takes the simple present tense ('rains').

questions.question: What is the difference between 'if' and 'in case'?

options.label: A
options.text: 'In case' describes taking a precaution BEFORE an event happens, while 'if' describes an action performed ONLY IF the event happens

options.label: B
options.text: 'In case' is only used in past tense

options.label: C
options.text: 'If' cannot be used with future time

questions.correct_answer_text: 'In case' describes taking a precaution BEFORE an event happens, while 'if' describes an action performed ONLY IF the event happens
questions.explanation: 'I'll take an umbrella in case it rains' (I take it now as a precaution) vs 'I'll open the umbrella if it rains' (only when rain begins).

questions.question: 'The bank will sanction the home loan provided that the applicant ______ a clean credit record.'
questions.explanation: 'The applicant' is third-person singular, taking the singular present verb 'submits' after 'provided that'.

questions.question: Complete the inversion: '______ I discovered the hidden truth earlier, I would have warned the committee.'
questions.explanation: An inverted past perfect third conditional begins with 'Had + subject + past participle' ('Had I discovered...').

topics.topic_name: Proverbs and Sentential Completions in Board Context

questions.question: Complete the famous proverb: 'Time and tide ______ for none.'
questions.explanation: The traditional idiomatic proverb treats 'Time and tide' as two distinct forces, taking the plural verb 'wait'.

questions.question: Complete the proverb: 'A stitch in time ______.'
questions.explanation: The proverb 'A stitch in time saves nine' means that timely remedial action prevents much larger problems later.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'Where there is a will, ______.'
questions.explanation: 'Where there is a will, there is a way' implies that determination will always find an avenue to accomplish a goal.

questions.question: Complete the saying: 'Strike the iron ______.'
questions.explanation: 'Strike the iron while it is hot' means to take immediate advantage of a favorable opportunity.

questions.question: 'United we stand, ______.'
questions.explanation: The universal proverb reminding us of the paramount necessity of social solidarity is 'United we stand, divided we fall.'
